html:
The long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies, from just after the Second World War to 1991. It was "cold" because the two never fought each other directly. They fought through arms races, spies, money, propaganda and wars in other countries.

The two sides split Europe: NATO in the West from 1949, the Warsaw Pact in the East from 1955. The Soviets tested their first atomic bomb (RDS-1) in 1949, and both built thousands of nuclear weapons. Sputnik 1 in 1957 began the race to space. The closest call came in 1962, when John F. Kennedy faced down Soviet missiles in Cuba.

The hot wars were fought elsewhere: in Korea, in the Vietnam War, in Angola and in Afghanistan after the Soviet invasion of 1979. In newly free Africa both sides backed leaders and coups; Patrice Lumumba of the Congo was one of the casualties. Rivalry reached into sport, chess and science.

Tension eased in the 1970s, when the Helsinki Accords fixed Europe's borders. In the 1980s Mikhail Gorbachev tried to reform the Soviet system. In 1989 the Berlin Wall fell and Eastern Europe broke free, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved in December 1991.
